title: ClientMessage
description: Anything a client sends to the daemon. One JSON object per line.

oneOf.description:
A device redeeming a pairing code, instead of a hello.

A device that is pairing has no token yet, so it cannot say hello. It sends this,
gets a [`PairResult`] or a refusal, and the connection is closed either way; the
paired device then connects again the ordinary way. Only the network port takes
this — pairing over the local socket would be pairing with oneself.

AudioFormat.description: Container format of one piece of audio on the wire.

oneOf.description: RIFF/WAVE with little-endian PCM16 samples.
Apple AIFF, which is what `say -o` writes.

Little-endian PCM16 samples with no container at all.

What a microphone hands a shell and what every recogniser wants. It is the shape the
first version of `voice_chunk` carried without naming it, which is why a dictation
that says nothing about its format is this one.

Opus packets in the length-prefixed framing described by [`OPUS_FRAMING`].

Not Ogg: an Ogg page carries granule positions and a checksum that a live stream over
an already-ordered, already-checked connection has no use for, and pulling one apart
on the phone would mean a second parser next to the codec.

Hello.description:
First message of every connection.

The client presents a token and nothing else; the daemon decides the role from it. A
client cannot claim to be human.

protocol_version.description:
The client's own protocol version. When `min_protocol_version` and
`max_protocol_version` are both present, this is only the client's preferred
version inside that range — the daemon does not read it and does not check that it
falls inside the range.

min_protocol_version.description:
Lowest protocol version this client can speak. A client built before this field
existed leaves it out, which the daemon reads as "exactly `protocol_version`"
(`DESIGN.md` § Architektur, Protokoll-Kompatibilität).

max_protocol_version.description:
Highest protocol version this client can speak. Same fallback as
`min_protocol_version`.

client_name.description: Free-text name of the client, for the connection list and the log.

audio_formats.description:
The formats this client can play a spoken answer in, best first.

The offering half of the format negotiation `DESIGN.md` § Mobil, Voice am Handy asks
for; [`crate::VoiceCapabilities`] on the `capabilities` answer is the half that says
what the daemon could do at all. It sits in the handshake because the choice holds
for the whole connection and because there is no round trip to spend on it: a client
that leaves it out is read as `wav` only, which is exactly what the first version
sent.

client_capabilities.description:
What this client shows the person beyond the conversation, as names such as
[`WORLD_EVENTS_CAPABILITY`].

Added 2026-09-14 for the workbench's worlds. The daemon says each thing a world needs
from the person once, and a notice sent to a client that does not show it is a notice
nobody heard: the CLI prints no event, the phone and the Linux shell know no
`world_event`. Only a connection that names [`WORLD_EVENTS_CAPABILITY`] here counts as
somebody listening. A name this daemon does not know is ignored, and a client that
leaves the field out declares nothing, which is what every client before it did.

AdapterId.description: Identifies a session adapter, for example `workbench` or `claude-code`.

AuftragId.description: Identifies a job file under `.companion/auftraege/<id>.json`. One path segment: see [`AuftragId::checked`] for what that rules out.

project.description: Absolute path of the project directory.

auftrag_id.description: Job file to hand to the session. The daemon passes the path, never the text.

prompt.description:
First message for a session that starts from a prompt rather than from a job file.
An adapter that drives a headless harness needs something to say; one that attaches
to an existing terminal ignores it.

SessionId.description: Identifies one session. Unique per machine only, assigned by the adapter that owns the session. See the collision rule on [`crate::MachineIdentity`].

ReadWindow.description: Which slice of a session's output to read.

oneOf.description: The last `lines` lines.
Everything from a byte offset a previous read returned.

Auftrag.description:
The job file, stored in the project under `.companion/auftraege/<id>.json`.

`DESIGN.md` § Datenmodelle lists this as: id, projekt, ziel, fertig_kriterium,
referenz, guardrails, gate_befehle, limits, loop_typ, modell, freigabe.

project.description: Absolute path of the project directory.

approval.description:
Absent until the person has approved the exact text. An unapproved job never
causes an outward action.

Reference.description: The reference a critic judges the result against.

GateCommand.description:
One gate command, split into program and arguments.

`DESIGN.md` § Sicherheit requires the daemon to run the approved text and nothing else,
without shell evaluation of variables or substitutions. Storing the command already
split is what makes that structural: there is no string for a shell to expand.

working_dir.description: Working directory for the command. Relative paths are resolved against the project.

Limits.description: Where a run has to stop even if it is not finished.

time_seconds.description:
Wall-clock limit. `DESIGN.md` § Loops names this the stand-in wherever the adapter
reports neither iterations nor tokens.

LoopType.description: Which loop discipline the orchestrator runs.

oneOf.description: One pass, the default.
Repeat until the done criterion holds or a limit is hit.
Builder and critic per part, against a reference.

Approval.description: The person's approval of one exact job text.

text_sha256.description: Hex-encoded SHA-256 of the approved job text, so a later edit invalidates it.

device.description: The device it came from, or absent for the shell at the machine.

confirmation.description:
How the person proved it was them. Absent means [`ApprovalConfirmation::Shell`],
which is what every approval written before this field existed was.

DeviceId.description: Identifies one paired device. Handed out when a pairing code is redeemed, and what a revocation names.

ApprovalConfirmation.description:
How the person proved it was them when they approved something.

`DESIGN.md` § Mobil, Freigaben vom Handy: "der Freigabe-Record vermerkt stets Gerät und
Bestätigungsart". At the machine the shell of the person is itself the proof — whoever
sits in front of an unlocked Mac is the person — which is what [`Self::Shell`] means and
why it is the default for a record written before this field existed. From a phone the
app says which of the three steps of that chapter it actually took, and [`Self::None`] is
a real answer rather than a missing one: the person chose that level and was warned.

oneOf.description: The desktop shell at the machine. There is no device and no second step.
Face ID or Touch ID immediately before sending.

The device passcode, which is what a device without biometrics falls back to and what
a high-risk setting demands whatever the level.

The app asked for nothing: whoever holds the unlocked phone approves.

Not accepted for an approval from a device (closed 2026-09-03, security review).
`DESIGN.md` § Mobil, Freigaben vom Handy asks for "immer mindestens die
Gerätecode-Bestätigung des Systems", and a device that could send this would be
deciding for itself that the sentence does not apply to it — the flag and the wish
come from the same client. It stays in the enum because a record written before that
day may carry it, and an audit trail does not get to rewrite what happened.

A kind this build does not know, out of a record a newer one wrote.

Never read as one of the four above, and [`Self::Shell`] least of all: an audit trail
that turned a confirmation it cannot name into "the person at the Mac" would be making
a claim about somebody. A request that carries this is refused rather than stored — a
client names a kind this daemon knows or gets no approval.

SessionStatus.description:
The status of one session.

`DESIGN.md` § Datenmodelle lists this as: id, adapter, maschine, projekt, modell,
zustand, laufzeit, kontext, budget, iteration, letzte_ausgabe, offene_frage,
auftrag_id. Every field an adapter may not know carries its origin instead of a
silently plausible zero.

machine.description:
Machine the session runs on, as the adapter reports it. `local` for this one.

Carries its origin since 2026-09-03. It used to be a bare `String` that defaulted to
`"local"`, and the workbench adapter filled that same `"local"` in whenever it could
not find out — a guess in the shape of a measurement, in the one field that decides
whether a session runs on this Mac or on the other machine. An adapter that does not
know now says so, and only one that does writes a value.

project.description: Absolute path of the project directory the session works in.

transcript_path.description:
Where the session writes its conversation, when whoever reports it knows.

Added 2026-09-03. Claude Code hands its hooks the `transcript_path` it writes itself,
which is the one authoritative answer to a question every reader of such a session
otherwise has to derive from a directory-naming rule that belongs to another program.
A reporter that does not know leaves it out, and the field is absent from the wire —
so a peer that predates it sends and reads exactly the bytes it always did.

last_activity_ms.description:
Unix time in milliseconds of the last sign of life the adapter saw from this session:
the last line of its stream, the last write to its state file, the last change to its
transcript.

Added 2026-09-03 for `done_limit`. A listing carries at most that many finished
sessions, and until now the daemon cut the tail off in the order the adapters happened
to hand it over — so a machine with weeks of history could answer with twenty sessions
that all ended in June while the one that ended a minute ago fell off the end. With
this field the daemon keeps the newest ones. An adapter that cannot say leaves it out,
and the field is absent from the wire, so a peer that predates it sends and reads
exactly the bytes it always did.

Not a [`Provenance`]: it is either a timestamp somebody read off the machine or it is
nothing. There is no estimate of it worth ordering a list by.

last_output.description: Last output of the session, trimmed to what the shell shows without asking.

open_question.description: The question the session is currently blocked on, if any.

permission_refused.description:
A tool call this session asked permission for and was refused automatically, by
policy — not a question `open_question` would have a person still answer, since the
agent was already told no before this was ever recorded.

Written out only when an adapter has one to report. A status that leaves it out is
read back as `None`, which is what keeps a daemon and a shell of different ages
speaking the same wire bytes: nothing an older peer sends changes meaning, and nothing
this build sends about a session it knows nothing more about grows a field.

kind.description:
Orchestrator or worker, for the list that shows only the first kind.

Written out only when an adapter knows it. A status that leaves it out is read back
as [`Provenance::Unknown`], which is what keeps a daemon and a shell of different
ages speaking the same wire bytes: nothing an older peer sends changes meaning, and
nothing this build sends about a session it knows nothing more about grows a field.

display_name.description:
What to call this session in a list, when the adapter has a name for it. The
workbench names its sessions and its workers; a bare terminal has nothing but an id.

machine_identity.description:
The machine this session runs on, stable across renames. See [`MachineIdentity`]
for the collision rule that makes this field load-bearing.

[`Self::machine`] stays what it was: the free-text name of the machine as the
adapter reports it, `local` for this one. The two are kept apart because the old
field is what a person reads and the new one is what a client keys on.

task_state.description:
Where the workbench task this session carries stands. Set only by the workbench's
carrier, which reports one session per task with `auftrag_id` set; every other reporter
leaves the five `task_*` fields out, and a status without them is written and read
exactly as before (added 2026-09-10, `AGENTS-PLAN.md` § 9 step 3).

task_reason.description:
Why the task stands where it does, in the carrier's own words: what it waits for, why
it is stuck, why an open task was not started.

task_title.description: The goal of the task, its first sentence. What the person calls the task.

task_wake_at.description: When a paused task goes on, as an RFC 3339 timestamp.

task_machine.description:
The machine the task's lead agent runs on right now. Apart from [`Self::machine`]
because the carrier that reports may run on another machine than the agent it carries.

Provenance.description:
A value together with where it came from.

`DESIGN.md` § Session-Adapter requires every status field to carry its origin, and the
session list to show an unknown field as unknown rather than as empty or zero. Making
`Unknown` a variant without a payload is what enforces that: there is no value to
mistake for a measurement.

oneOf.description: Read from a structured channel: a hook, a status file, an adapter report.
Derived or guessed, for example a token count extrapolated from elapsed time.
The adapter cannot supply this field at all.

SessionState.description:
What a session is doing right now.

`DESIGN.md` § Session-Adapter wants unknown things shown as unknown rather than as
something plausible, and this field is where an adapter is most tempted to guess. An
adapter that only sees a live terminal knows the session exists, not what it is doing:
that is [`SessionState::Unknown`]. One whose session has simply vanished knows it is
over but not how it went: that is [`SessionState::Lost`].

oneOf.description: Waiting for input from the person, including an open question.
Finished its work. Only for an adapter that saw it finish.
The session is there, but the adapter cannot tell what it is doing.

The session is gone and the adapter never learned how it ended. Over, but not
finished: a crash and a clean end look the same from the outside.

SessionKind.description:
What kind of agent a session is.

`DESIGN.md` § Mobil, Sessionansicht: the session list of the phone shows orchestrators
and hides workers, because supervising workers is the orchestrator's job and not the
companion's. An adapter that cannot tell the two apart says so by leaving the field
[`Provenance::Unknown`] — there is no third variant here, because "unknown" is what the
origin of every status field already means, and two ways of saying it would let a
filter answer differently depending on which one an adapter picked. A list that hides
workers therefore hides exactly `Measured(Worker)` and `Estimated(Worker)`, and shows
everything else.

oneOf.description: Drives other sessions and answers to the person.
Was started by an orchestrator and reports back to it.

MachineIdentity.description:
Which machine a session runs on, in a form that survives a rename.

**The collision rule for session ids.** A [`SessionId`] is unique on the machine that
issued it and nowhere else: two machines both running the workbench in
`~/AI/companion` produce the very same id for two different sessions. A client that
speaks to more than one daemon — the phone in the aggregation mode of `DESIGN.md`
§ Mobil — therefore keys every session by the pair (`machine.id`, `id`) and never by
the id alone. Where the machine identity is unknown, the pair cannot be formed, and the
client falls back to the connection it received the session on, which is unique within
one client run. The daemon never rewrites an id to make it globally unique: the id is
what a person sees and what every command names, and a prefix that changed per client
would break both.

id.description:
Stable and opaque. Generated once per machine and kept, so a renamed machine is
still recognised as the same one.

display_name.description:
What to call the machine in a list. Free text a person may change at any time, and
never the thing two sessions are told apart by.

MachineId.description: Identifies one machine, stable across restarts and independent of its name. Generated once, never derived from a hostname: a hostname changes with a network and collides between two machines set up the same way.

TaskState.description:
Where a task of the workbench stands, as its carrier reports it.

The states of `claude-workbench/docs/AGENTS-PLAN.md` § 2, "gleichlautend in Ansicht, Datei
und Companion", spelled as the wire names the carrier (`wb-traeger`) sends. A task is not a
session: the carrier reports one session per task with `auftrag_id` set, and this is what
that task is doing, which [`SessionState`] cannot say — "paused until the quota resets" is
neither waiting for the person nor idle, and "ready for acceptance" is not done.

Reading accepts every `wartet_auf_*` spelling as [`TaskState::WartetAufNutzer`]: carriers
from before the rename name the person they wait for in the wire value.

oneOf.description: In the backlog, not started yet.
The lead agent is alive and was seen at the last tick.

A display without an automatic consequence: a deadline passed without progress, or the
lead agent is gone and could not be revived.
Paused until the subscription quota resets.
Paused for the night window.
Paused until a wake time the lead agent left behind.
A question, an approval or a conflict only the person can settle.
Result checked, reviewer run, report written.
The lead agent holds the task for unsolvable as it stands.
A local lead agent handed the task back because it is beyond the model.
Accepted by the person.
Discarded by the person.

VoiceId.description: Identifies one dictation or one spoken answer. Assigned by the daemon, so a client cannot address a stream that is not its own.

TurnId.description: Identifies one turn of the companion's own chat: one confirmation, or one background report. Assigned by the daemon, so two turns running at once never share an id and their events never mix on the wire.

EndpointRole.description:
What an endpoint is used for.

The list is the one from `DESIGN.md` § Endpoints. A role points at a provider profile,
and several roles may point at the same one: local, a second machine on the network and
cloud are only different URLs.

oneOf.description: The model the companion itself talks with.

The companion's own helper model: the web research of `web_research` and the
shortening of long tool results. Not the model a spawned session runs on — that
stands in the order the session is started with.
Speech to text.
Text to speech.
The local wakeword detector.
Speech to speech, an optional mode rather than the standard path.

Settings.description:
Everything the daemon reads out of its settings file.

`PartialEq` only, not `Eq`: [`LocationSettings`] carries an `f64` coordinate, and `f64`
has no total order to found an `Eq` on.

tool_boundary.description:
Boundary for the companion's own tools, everything that is not high risk.
`DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 13.

agent_boundary.description:
Boundary a spawned session runs under. `DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 2.

A second field rather than the same one, because the two are different questions:
what the companion may do itself, and what it may let an agent do.

enabled_adapters.description:
Adapters the daemon should load. Empty means every adapter it was built with,
with one exception: an adapter that is opt-in stays off until it is named here by
its id. The generic terminal adapter ([`PTY_ADAPTER_ID`]) is the one, because
`DESIGN.md` § Sicherheit says a permission level cannot restrict a foreign CLI —
nobody is to end up with one by accident.

pty_command.description:
The command the generic terminal adapter runs, program first, arguments after.
Empty is the default and means it starts nothing: there is no sensible default
program for "any CLI".

adapter_voice.description:
The speech path per connected agent, keyed by adapter id.

An adapter that is not named here uses [`VoicePath::Companion`], so a newly
connected harness is never silently left mute — see [`Settings::voice_path`].
`DESIGN.md` § Session-Adapter, addendum of 2026-08-24.

As of 2026-08-24 the value has no effect anywhere; see [`VoicePath`].

notification_channels.description:
Where the person is told about something. The figure alone by default: every other
channel either makes noise or leaves the machine.
`DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 12.

forward_done.description:
Whether a finished session is worth telling the person about. On by default, because
a run that is done is the one thing somebody is actually waiting for.

done_handling.description:
What happens with a finished run beyond telling the person.
`DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 11. [`Self::forward_done`] says whether the
person hears about it at all, this says what else runs.

inventory_allowed.description:
Whether the companion may read what is installed — skills, tools, MCP servers,
workflows. `DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 4, and § Sicherheit: reading a
working directory is reading somebody's work, so it stays off until it is allowed.

budget_limit_percent.description:
Share of the budget at which the companion stops starting anything new, in per cent.
Zero means no limit. `DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 7.

selected_skill_level.description:
The tier last applied successfully after a human choice. An older document has no
marker, so the default `recommended` never installs merely because the daemon started.
Managed by the daemon after installation, not trusted from the wire.

conversation_style.description: `DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 8: how much he says.

address_form.description: `DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 8: how he addresses the person.

figure_name.description:
`DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 8: what the figure is called. The companion
writes in this name, which is why it is the daemon's and not only the window's.

introduced.description:
Whether the figure has already introduced itself by name.

`DESIGN.md` § Ausbau, "Name und Persona": the figure introduces itself with the name
somebody gave it — once, at its first appearance after the setup, and never again
unasked. The mark belongs here rather than in the preferences of a shell, for the
reason `TASKS.md` "Erststart" already wrote down about the setup itself: a mark that
only the shell holds survives a wiped configuration directory, and a freshly set up
figure would then never say hello. A shell sets this the moment it has said it.

network.description:
The network listener a phone connects through. Off at the factory.
`DESIGN.md` § Mobil, Ferntransport.

voice_server.description: The local speech server the daemon starts on demand. Off at the factory.

location.description:
Where the `weather` and `places` tools take "here" from, when a call does not name a
place of its own. `DESIGN.md` § Ausbau, "Werkzeugkatalog".

weather_enabled.description:
Whether the `weather` tool may run at all. `DESIGN.md` § Werkzeugkatalog: every
network tool is "einzeln abschaltbar". On by default — Open-Meteo needs no key and
the tool answers only what the person's own location setting already names.

places_enabled.description:
Whether the `places` tool (geocoding and routes) may run at all. Same reasoning as
[`Self::weather_enabled`].

web_research_enabled.description:
Whether the `web_research` tool may run at all — the one tool that asks the open
internet a question in the person's own words rather than sending a coordinate.
Same reasoning as [`Self::weather_enabled`], and on by default for the same one:
it needs no key of its own, it runs through whichever subagent the person has
already configured, and `tool_boundary = read_only` switches it off along with the
other two outward tools regardless of what stands here.

proactive.description:
What the companion watches for on its own, and where each threshold sits.
`DESIGN.md` § Ausbau, "Volle Proaktivität". All four classes on at the factory —
see [`ProactiveSettings`] for why this one defaults to on where the rest default off.

subagent_condensation_enabled.description:
Whether a tool step classified `slow` has its already-gated local result condensed
through a subagent. `DESIGN.md` § Wechselspiel und Ansprechbarkeit names this class
of tool by an expectation, not a measured duration — there is no clock behind this
switch either, which is why it reads as on/off rather than as a number of seconds:
a duration here would promise a precision this program does not have. Off means
every tool step runs in the daemon itself, whatever its class, which stays a
background task either way and never blocks the chat.

worlds.description: Where the workbench's agent worlds are read from. See [`WorldsSettings`].

ToolBoundary.description: How far the companion may act on its own with a class of tools.

oneOf.description: Read, never write.
Ask before every use. The default everywhere.
Act without asking.

HighRiskSettings.description:
The three tool classes that reach outside the machine. `DESIGN.md` § Sicherheit puts
them on `ask` and lets only the person raise them, with a warning.

No tool of `companion-brain` sends mail, pushes to a phone or publishes anything yet
(2026-09-03) — these three fields travel with the settings document and the shell can
show and raise them, but nothing reads them: they take effect only once the matching
tool exists. The guard against a future tool of one of these classes shipping without
also reading its field is a test over
`companion_brain::tools::ToolBox::ungated_high_risk_specs`.

mail.description: No effect until a mail tool exists — see the struct doc above.

push.description: No effect until a push tool exists — see the struct doc above.

publish.description: No effect until a publish tool exists — see the struct doc above.

VoicePath.description:
Which speech path one connected agent uses.

`DESIGN.md` § Session-Adapter, addendum of 2026-08-24: an agent that brings its own
speech may keep it, and the companion then passes text and control through without
listening or speaking for that agent. An agent without speech of its own gets the
companion's pipeline in front of it, which is why that is the default here.

This is an ordinary setting, deliberately not a high-risk one: both paths speak on the
same machine to the same person, and neither widens what runs unasked. It therefore
stays out of [`Settings::high_risk_changes`].

**Nothing acts on this yet (2026-08-24).** The value is stored, checked, carried over
the socket and read back by the shell, but no part of the voice pipeline asks for it:
`passthrough` today leaves the companion's microphone and voice exactly where
`companion` leaves them. The wiring belongs to the voice integration. Until it lands,
somebody who sets `passthrough` and still hears the companion is not looking at a bug
in this field.

oneOf.description:
The companion's own speech pipeline runs in front of the agent: it listens for the
person, hands the agent text, and says the agent's answers itself. The default,
because an agent that cannot speak is left mute by any other choice.

The agent keeps its own speech. The companion passes text and control through and
keeps its own microphone and voice out of this agent's way, so the two never talk
over each other.

NotificationChannel.description: Where the companion may reach a person. `DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 12.

oneOf.description:
The character on the screen. The only channel that never leaves the machine, and
therefore the only one that is on by default.
A short sound next to the figure.
Said out loud, over the configured speech output.
A notification of the operating system, seen even when the figure is covered.
A push message to a phone.
An email.

DoneHandling.description:
What happens when a session reports that it is done.
`DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 11.

oneOf.description: The person is told, and nothing else happens. The sparing default.
The gate commands of the job file run, and their verdict is reported with it.
A second session reviews the result before the person sees it.

Autonomy.description:
How far the companion acts on its own when a session reports something.
`DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 3.

oneOf.description: Watch and report, decide nothing. The default.
Answer what is unambiguous, ask about the rest.
Answer and act within the guardrails of the job file.

SkillLevel.description:
How much of the skill package goes into a recognised harness.
`DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 10.

oneOf.description: Nothing is installed.
The obligatory core.
The core and the checked extensions.

ConversationStyle.description: How much the companion says. `DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 8.

AddressForm.description: How the companion addresses the person. `DESIGN.md` § Ersteinrichtung, point 8.

oneOf.description: German "du", English first name.

EndpointConfig.description:
The endpoint part of the settings: the profiles, and which role uses which of them.

The schema deliberately advertises the empty configuration as the default, not the one
`Default::default` builds: that one depends on the operating system the daemon runs on
(see below), and a generated schema that changes with its build host is not a contract.
What a given daemon actually starts with is a runtime matter and reaches the client in
`settings_get`, never through a schema annotation.

EndpointProfile.description: One provider profile: how to reach a backend, and under which name its key lives.

id.description: Name the role bindings and the settings page use.

url.description:
Base URL for a protocol that speaks HTTP, for example
`http://127.0.0.1:8765`. For [`EndpointProtocol::Cli`] it is the absolute path of
the program instead.

key_ref.description:
Name under which the key lives in the the secret store of the daemon, never the
key itself. Absent for a local endpoint that needs none.

Since 2026-09-03 this name is the profile's own [`Self::id`] and nothing else — see
[`Self::key_name`] for why, and [`EndpointConfig::borrowed_keys`] for what refuses a
document that says otherwise. The field stays because it is what says *whether* a
profile needs a key at all, and because a configuration written before that date is
migrated by reading it.

model.description:
Model this profile uses. `DESIGN.md` § Endpoints wants the settings page to show it
for every profile.

voice.description:
Voice this profile speaks with, when the caller names none.

A speech endpoint has its own set of voice names, and the OpenAI ones are not
among them: Kokoro, the local default here, knows `af_heart` and refuses `alloy`
mid-answer. That belongs next to the model, for the same reason the model does —
which voices exist is a property of the profile, not of the sentence being spoken.

args.description: Fixed arguments for a CLI profile, in front of whatever the driver adds.

language.description:
The spoken language this profile is good at, as a lowercase ISO code (`"de"`).

`DESIGN.md` § Voice ties language to the model, not to the app, so this is the one
place that says which language a TTS profile actually speaks well. Absent for a
profile that was never told — Kokoro's `af_heart` reads any text handed to it, German
included, just badly, and nothing here claims otherwise on its behalf. The TTS role
chain uses it to move a matching profile to the front for a sentence detected as that
language; a profile nobody tagged keeps its configured place.

reasoning_effort.description:
How much a reasoning model may think before it writes the answer, as the
OpenAI-compatible `reasoning_effort` field. Absent for every profile that never asked
for it, and then nothing is sent at all.

Opt-in for the same reason `stream_options.include_usage` is not sent: a server that
does not know a field answers the whole request with 400, and a chat that fails over
a knob nobody set would be the worse trade. Measured 2026-09-05 on this machine, both
local servers behind `wb-modell-proxy`: without it, `qwen3.8-27b` over
`mlx_vlm.server` and `ornith:9b` over Ollama spend their whole answer in
`reasoning_content`/`reasoning`, which this protocol does not carry — the person sees
a first token after 30 seconds, or none at all. With `"none"` the first visible token
arrives after half a second on the 9B. It is a string rather than an enum because the
set of accepted values belongs to the server, not to this program.

EndpointProtocol.description:
How the daemon talks to an endpoint.

`DESIGN.md` § Endpoints separates two execution models: an API profile, where the
daemon speaks the interface itself and can stream, and a CLI profile, where it drives
`claude -p` or `codex exec` and uses the subscription without a key. [`Self::Cli`] is
that second model; every other variant is the first.

oneOf.description:
The OpenAI HTTP shape: `/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/audio/transcriptions`,
`/v1/audio/speech`. What most local servers and most providers speak.
The Anthropic Messages API.
Ollama's own API under `/api`.
A `whisper.cpp` server: `/inference` with a multipart upload, plain text back.
A local program the daemon starts, no HTTP and no key.

RoleBinding.description: Which profile serves a role, and which ones to try when it fails.

fallback.description: Tried in order after the primary one failed.

NetworkSettings.description:
The TCP/TLS listener a phone reaches the daemon through.

`DESIGN.md` § Mobil, Ferntransport: off at the factory, and switching it on is a
high-risk setting — at the network port the UID check of the Unix socket falls away, and
what is left is the certificate and the token. The role `agent` does not exist there at
all; a remote orchestrator keeps reporting to the daemon on its own machine.

enabled.description: Off unless a person turned it on, with the warning in front of them.

advertise_address.description:
The address a pairing tells a device to connect to, when that is not the address
the daemon binds. Empty means they are the same.

A wildcard bind says which interfaces the daemon accepts on, not where anybody can
reach it, and a daemon behind a forwarded port or a dynamic name is reached under
something it never sees. Both cases put the reachable address here.

VoiceServerSettings.description:
The local speech server the daemon starts when it needs one.

`DESIGN.md` § Voice puts the speech models behind endpoint profiles, and the local ones
live in a server that has to be running before the first word. Expecting somebody to
have started it is what made the voice path fail with "connection refused" instead of
speaking; expecting the daemon to keep it running all day would hold a model in memory
for the twenty-three hours nobody talks.

So: started at the first voice request, waited for, and stopped again after a
configurable idle. Off at the factory, because starting a program named in a file is
something a person decides — the same reasoning as for the terminal adapter, and the
same warning when it is switched on.

enabled.description: Off unless a person turned it on, with the warning in front of them.

command.description:
Program and arguments, program first. There is no default program: which server
serves the local models is a choice, and guessing one would start something nobody
asked for.

env.description:
Environment variables for it, on top of the daemon's own.

`HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` is set by the daemon whatever stands here: a speech server that
reaches for a model download on the first request turns a spoken sentence into a
network call nobody asked for. Naming it here anyway is allowed and changes nothing.

ready_url.description:
The URL the daemon asks until the server answers, for example
`http://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/models`. Any answer counts as ready, including an error
status: what is being established is that the server is listening and serving, not
that this particular route exists.

startup_timeout_seconds.description:
How long the daemon waits for it to answer before it gives up and says so. Loading a
speech model takes seconds to tens of seconds, so this is generous by default.

idle_timeout_seconds.description:
How long without a voice request before the server is stopped again. Zero keeps it
running for as long as the daemon does.

LocationSettings.description:
Where a coordinate for the weather and places tools comes from, when a call does not name
a place of its own. `DESIGN.md` § Ausbau, "Werkzeugkatalog": "Standort kommt aus der
macOS-Ortung … wenn freigegeben", with manual coordinates as the alternative it names
first — "Ort/Koordinaten in Settings".

allow_system_location.description:
Off unless a person turned it on. `DESIGN.md` § Ausbau: "Ortung ist eine eigene,
standardmäßig AUS-Einstellung." Even switched on, this only allows the daemon to ask
the operating system for a position at all — the system's own dialog, not this flag,
decides whether it actually gets one.

place_name.description:
A place name, shown back to the person; carries no meaning for the tools themselves,
which read only the coordinates below.

ProactiveSettings.description:
What the companion watches for on its own, and where each of the four thresholds sits.

`DESIGN.md` § Ausbau, "Volle Proaktivität": "Session hängt auffällig lange, Budget wird
eng, ein Termin rückt heran, der Morgen-Überblick beim ersten Erscheinen. Jede Meldeklasse
ist einzeln abschaltbar."

All four are on at the factory, unlike every other switch of this document that decides
what the companion may do by itself. Watching and saying so is the *bottom* rung of
§ Verhalten, "Eigene Autonomie" — the rung [`Autonomy::Observe`] is named after — so a
person who never touched a setting has a companion that reports, which is what they
installed it for. Nothing here acts: the four notices are sentences, and the only thing
they cost is the person's attention, which is what the thresholds are for.

session_stalled.description:
A session busy without a sign of life for longer than
[`Self::stalled_after_minutes`].

appointment_soon.description:
An appointment starting within [`Self::appointment_lead_minutes`]. Silent without the
calendar permission, and it never asks for one of its own accord: a dialog nobody
opened is exactly the unasked interruption this whole section is careful about.

morning_briefing.description: The overview at the first appearance of the day.

stalled_after_minutes.description:
How long a session may be busy without any sign of life before it counts as stuck.

Twenty minutes because a long tool step, a big test suite and a model that is thinking
all look exactly like a hung session from the outside for several minutes at a time;
under that, the notice would be about the companion's impatience rather than about the
session. Zero switches the class off the same way [`Self::session_stalled`] does — a
threshold of nothing would make every busy session stuck.

budget_percent.description:
Share of the budget, in per cent, past which the companion says so. Zero switches the
class off, for the same reason as above.

Not [`Settings::budget_limit_percent`], which is the share at which the companion
stops *starting* things: a person may well want to hear about it long before anything
is refused, and hearing about it at the moment work stops is too late to plan around.

appointment_lead_minutes.description: How many minutes before an appointment the notice comes. Zero switches the class off.

report_sessions_needing_me.description:
Whether one line goes into the conversation when a session needs the person: it has
asked something, it waits for input, or a permission was refused for it.

Off at the factory, unlike the four classes above, and the only one of these values
that writes into the chat history at all. `DESIGN.md` § Chat-Hygiene, 2026-09-05: the
history is the conversation, and what a session reports about itself belongs in the
notice log — "es sei denn, der Mensch hat `report_sessions_needing_me` eingeschaltet,
dann genau eine Zeile je Anlass". He says when he wants it; until he does, the figure
and the session list carry the news on their own.

task_events.description:
Whether the companion addresses a workbench task that needs the person — it asks
something, it waits for acceptance, or its lead agent gave it up — with a tone, a
banner and a spoken sentence (`ProactiveClass::TaskEvent`).

Off at the factory, and only the person switches it: "Ob der Companion eine Aufgabe,
die ihn braucht, von sich aus anspricht, hängt an seinem Schalter, der ab Werk aus ist
und den nur Skryx-L-A stellt" (`claude-workbench/docs/AGENTS-PLAN.md` § 6). Off does not
hide a task: every event of one still goes into the notice log and to the figure, and
the session list and the morning overview carry where each task stands.

world_events.description:
Whether the companion addresses what a workbench world needs from the person — an
open question of its lead agent, a message an agent marked as a question or a result
for the person — with a tone, a banner and a spoken sentence
(`ProactiveClass::WorldEvent`).

Off at the factory, for the reason [`Self::task_events`] is: the plan makes the
companion the way these reach the person (`claude-workbench/docs/AGENTS-PLAN.md` § 7),
and whether that way makes a sound is the person's switch. Off does not hide
anything: every such item still goes into the notice log and to the figure, the
morning overview counts them, and the companion reads them out when asked.

WorldsSettings.description:
Where the agent worlds of the workbench are read from (`claude-workbench/docs/AGENTS-PLAN.md`
§ 7: the companion is the way "braucht dich" reaches the person, and a player in the
world's channel).

Read only through the workbench's own programs — `wb-welt finden`, `wb-welt ansicht`,
`wb-kanal`, `wb-ticket` — and never by opening a world's files: the world has one writer,
its data library, and a reader that bypassed it would see half-written transactions the
library's own view hides.

enabled.description:
Whether the daemon reads worlds at all. On at the factory: it only reads, a machine
without the workbench's programs simply has no worlds, and the companion being the
way a world's question reaches the person is the plan, not an extra.

poll_seconds.description: How often the worlds are read, in seconds. At least [`MIN_WORLD_POLL_SECONDS`].

sources.description: The machines whose worlds are read. This machine alone at the factory.

WorldSource.description: One machine whose worlds the companion reads, and how to ask it.

machine.description:
[`LOCAL_WORLD_MACHINE`] for this machine, otherwise the ssh destination the
workbench's programs run on (`peer`, `ich@peer`). The companion uses the ssh this
account already has, with its keys and its configuration; it adds no transport of
its own.

cli_dir.description:
The directory holding `wb-welt`, `wb-kanal`, `wb-ticket` and `agents_traeger.py`, on
that machine. Empty looks them up on the `PATH`. A leading `~/` is that machine's
home directory.

roots.description:
Directories whose subfolders are searched for a project world (`wb-welt finden
--wurzel`). Empty together with [`Self::projects`] leaves the workbench's own
default, `~/AI`.

global.description: The global world (`--global`). Empty leaves the workbench's own default.

DeviceLevel.description:
What a paired device may do.

The same two levels as the remote machines of `DESIGN.md` § Sicherheit. A phone does not
get the full command set by being a phone; the person picks the level when they pair it.

oneOf.description:
Read the session list, read output, read the settings. Nothing that changes anything.
The default, because the careful half of a choice is the one a missing field lands on.
Everything the person's own shell may do, approvals included.

RequestEnvelope.description: A request with the id its response will carry.

oneOf.description:
The sessions the daemon knows, filtered.

A machine that has been working for weeks has hundreds of finished sessions, and a
session list that shows all of them is unusable. The filter is part of the request
rather than of the shell, so every client gets the same short answer.

running_only.description: Only sessions that are still going: busy, idle or waiting.

done_limit.description:
How many finished sessions to include at most. Ignored when `running_only` is
set.

oneOf.description: Cut the running turn short. The session stays alive and can be talked to again.

adapter.description: A single adapter, or all of them when absent.

oneOf.description: Writes a job file into a project. The file is not approved by writing it.

project.description: Absolute path of the project directory.

oneOf.description:
Approves the exact content the person was shown.

The hash is what the shell computed over the canonical form of the file it
displayed. The daemon canonicalises the file again and refuses if the two differ:
that is what ties the approval to the text somebody actually read.

confirmation.description:
How the person proved it was them, for the record in the register.

Absent from the local socket means the shell of the person at the machine, which
is what an approval there has always been. From a device it is required and may
not be `shell`: `DESIGN.md` § Mobil, Freigaben vom Handy wants the record to say
which device approved and how, and an app that says nothing gets no approval
rather than a record that looks like one made at the Mac.

oneOf.description:
Run one gate command of an approved job file, named by its position in the list.

`project`, `auftrag_id` and `expected_hash` are what make this safe, and a request
without them is refused. They are optional in the schema only so that a client
written against the earlier shape still parses; it will be told what is missing
rather than silently running something.

session_id.description: The session the result belongs to, for the event. Not where the command runs.

oneOf.description: An orchestrator writes the status of its own session.

status.description: Boxed to keep the size of every other request down.

oneOf.description: An orchestrator asks the person something through the companion.
An orchestrator reports progress or a finished result.

Brings the local speech server up before anybody speaks, and does nothing else.

The shell sends this the moment the wakeword fires, one step ahead of
[`Self::VoiceBegin`]. Measured on this machine (`tests/voice-latency/README.md`, the
section on the real speech path), a cold server costs 309 to 562 milliseconds of the
1.5 second budget `DESIGN.md` § Voice sets for an answer, and it is cold every time
somebody has been quiet for longer than `voice_server.idle_timeout_seconds`. The word
itself is spoken before the sentence is, so the loading fits in the gap.

It starts nothing the settings do not ask for: a daemon whose `voice_server` is
switched off answers without doing anything, the same as [`Self::VoiceBegin`] would.
There is deliberately no warm-up in the idle case — how much memory the machine gives
up while nobody is talking is a decision for the person, not for this request.

Opens one dictation. The daemon answers with the id every chunk of it carries.

There is no voice activity detection behind this: the shell decides where an
utterance begins and ends, the daemon transcribes what it is given. That keeps the
endpointing next to the microphone, where the audio and the barge-in state are.

sample_rate_hz.description:
For `pcm16` the rate the samples were recorded at; for `opus` the rate the daemon
decodes to, which has to be one of [`crate::OPUS_SAMPLE_RATES`]. An Opus stream
carries no rate of its own — the encoder on the phone may well have run at 48 kHz
and the decoder still produce the 16 kHz a recogniser wants.

language.description:
Language hint for the endpoint. Absent means the endpoint decides, which is
what `DESIGN.md` § Voice wants: the language hangs on the model, not on the app.

format.description:
What the chunks of this dictation carry. Absent means [`AudioFormat::Pcm16`],
which is what the first version sent without naming it.

oneOf.description:
One piece of recorded audio, base64 encoded.

Two field names for one payload, and exactly one of them is written. `pcm16_base64`
is the field of the first version and still the one a PCM16 dictation uses;
`audio_base64` carries anything else, Opus above all. Keeping the old name rather
than widening its meaning is what lets a daemon of either age read a PCM16 chunk, and
what stops an old daemon from taking Opus packets for samples and handing a
recogniser noise.

Ends the dictation. The transcript arrives as an `stt_final` event, not in the
response: a client that waits for the answer to this request would block for as
long as the endpoint takes.

Speaks a text. The audio arrives as `tts_chunk` events, the end as `tts_done`.

Splitting an answer into sentences happens above this: here one call is one piece
of text, and the caller decides how much of it to hand over at a time.

voice.description: Voice name to pass to the endpoint, when it has more than one.

oneOf.description:
Stops a spoken answer that is still running.

Only the connection that asked for it may stop it: a spoken answer belongs to
whoever requested it, and the phone must not be able to silence the shell on the
machine. An id that is not running any more — or belongs to somebody else — is
answered with `unknown_session`, which is the same answer either way and therefore
tells a stranger nothing about what somebody else is having spoken.

The daemon stops the synthesis, drops what has not been sent yet and closes the
stream with a `tts_done` carrying [`crate::SpeechEnd::Cancelled`].

The person says something to the companion.

The answer arrives as `chat_delta`, `chat_tool` and `chat_done` events, not in the
response: a client that waited for the answer here would block for the whole turn,
tool calls included. The response itself carries the id of the turn this message
started (`ResponseBody::ChatStarted`), which is what lets a client tell its own
question's events apart from a background report of an earlier one — both can be
under way at once, since a `chat_message` that arrives while a tool step of an
earlier one is still running is answered rather than refused (`DESIGN.md` §
Wechselspiel und Ansprechbarkeit). Only the human role may send this — an answer is
written by the model that speaks for the person, and a docked orchestrator that
could ask for one would be talking to the companion in the person's name.

voice.description: Whether the answer should also be spoken. `chat_done` says whether it was.

oneOf.description:
Stops the background report of one exchange — the turn id a `chat_message` was
answered with.

`DESIGN.md` § Wechselspiel und Ansprechbarkeit lets an answer that needs a tool step
confirm at once and report afterwards. Until this request existed, the only way to say
"this one report, not any more" was to close the connection, which stops every report
of that client and the conversation with it. The answer says whether there was one to
stop; an exchange that already finished, or never deferred, is not an error.

Only the human role may send it, for the same reason `chat_message` is the human's:
the report belongs to the person who asked for it, and a docked orchestrator that
could cancel one would be silencing an answer meant for somebody else.
Measures the configured endpoints and returns what the probe found.

role.description: Only the profiles of one role, or every configured profile when absent.

oneOf.description:
The settings document the daemon is working with.

Only the person's shell may ask. The document carries no key — a profile holds the
name of a keychain entry and nothing else — but it does say what this machine is
allowed to do without asking, and that is not something a docked orchestrator gets
to read.

Replaces the settings document.

The daemon checks it the same way it checks the file at load time and writes it
atomically with mode 0600, or refuses the whole document and changes nothing. A
change that *raises* a permission needs `confirm_high_risk`, and only a person can
give it: `DESIGN.md` § Sicherheit puts mail, push and publish on `ask` and says only
the person may put them on `full`, with a warning. The companion itself has no tool
that sends this request, which is what keeps that promise on the daemon side rather
than in a prompt.

settings.description: Boxed to keep the size of every other request down.

confirm_high_risk.description:
True only where a person confirmed the warning for the raise this document
contains. Absent means false, so an older client can never raise anything.

oneOf.description:
Applies the skill tier already stored by the daemon. Only the person's local shell
may ask; no tier or target path comes from the request.

Opens a pairing: a short-lived one-time code a device redeems over the network port.

Only the person's own shell and the CLI tool may ask, both of which reach the daemon
through the local Unix socket. The level is decided here, at the machine, and not by
the device that redeems the code (`DESIGN.md` § Mobil, Geräte-Token).

device_name.description: What the device will be called in the list.

oneOf.description:
The person decides who answers one session's questions.

`DESIGN.md` § Verhalten, "Fragen der Orchestratoren": "Je Session laesst sich 'immer
mich fragen' setzen." It is a decision about a session, not a setting of the daemon,
so it lives next to the session and not in the settings document — and it belongs to
the person, not to the session, which is why the register keeps it outside anything a
commanded session can write.

It overrules the autonomy rung in one direction only: a session marked this way is
never answered by the companion itself, whatever the rung says. It can never make the
companion answer something it otherwise would not.

Every session the person put on "always ask me".

A listing rather than one lookup per row: a shell draws the whole session list at
once and would otherwise need one request per session to know which switch is on.
The paired devices, revoked ones included.
Revokes one device. Its live connections are cut at once, not at the next handshake.

The register: what ran, when, what it left behind, what it answered on its own and
what it cost.

`DESIGN.md` § Verhalten, "Fragen der Orchestratoren": "jede Selbstantwort wird im
Register mit Frage, Antwort und Quelle protokolliert und ist im Panel nachlesbar."
Until this request existed the register was write-only from the socket — the daemon
filled it and nothing could read it back, so the panel that sentence promises had
nothing to show.

Only the person's shell may ask, for the same reason `get_settings` is theirs: the
register names every project this machine worked in, quotes what sessions reported,
and says what each of them cost. A docked orchestrator gets to report about its own
session, not to read the history of everybody else's.

project.description: Only rows of this project. Compared as the string the adapter reported.

since_ms.description: Only rows that started at or after this Unix time in milliseconds.

until_ms.description: Only rows that started before this Unix time in milliseconds.

with_self_answers.description: Only rows that carry at least one self-answer.

limit.description: At most this many rows, newest first. Zero means the daemon's own default.

oneOf.description:
The person heard or read a notice that carried an `ack`.

Added 2026-09-14 for the workbench's worlds: a message an agent marked as a question
or a result for the person stays "braucht dich" in its world until it is acknowledged
(`wb-kanal quittieren --agent mensch`), and whether the sentence was heard to its end or
the banner was opened is something only the shell knows. The daemon looks the `ack` up
among the notices it published itself; one it does not know is refused, so a client
cannot acknowledge a delivery the daemon never announced.

Only the person's shell, never a docked orchestrator: acknowledging is saying the
person has seen it.

The shell showed the person a notice that carried a `notice_id`.

Added 2026-09-14 for the workbench's worlds, as the second half of
[`WORLD_EVENTS_CAPABILITY`]: the daemon counts an item as said only once a shell that
shows world notices confirms it put this one in front of the person. Until then the
next shell that connects gets it again. Showing is not reading: a marked message stays
open in its world until `acknowledge_notice`.

Only from a connection that declared [`WORLD_EVENTS_CAPABILITY`] in its `Hello`.

PairRequest.description:
A device redeeming a pairing code. The first and only message such a connection sends.

The name of the device is not in here on purpose: it was chosen by the person at the
machine when they created the pairing, and a device that could name itself could name
itself anything.

code.description: The long code out of the QR, or the short one from the same pairing.
